claims.text: Controlled thermal processing can tune the extent of nanoscale chemical short-range ordering in the lightweight HEA.
Rapid quenching produces a disordered solid solution with minimal nanoscale chemical ordering.
An intermediate degree of chemical ordering maintains a uniform distribution of alloying elements.
Uniform elemental distribution promotes formation of a continuous, self-passivating Al2O3/Cr2O3 oxide layer during high-temperature exposure.
A dense, continuous Al2O3/Cr2O3 layer protects the substrate and enhances oxidation resistance at 900 °C.
An intermediate degree of chemical ordering enhances solid-solution strengthening.
Intermediate chemical ordering enables low density, high strength, corrosion resistance, and oxidation resistance to be obtained simultaneously.
Minimal ordering fails to maximize the interactions responsible for passivation and strengthening.
Excessive ordering leads to incipient phase segregation or second-phase formation.
Phase segregation disrupts uniform elemental distribution and causes heterogeneous oxide-scale formation.
Phase segregation compromises mechanical strength and corrosion resistance.
Relative to a rapidly quenched baseline, samples with intermediate ordering will have lower oxidation mass gain at 900 °C.
Relative to a rapidly quenched baseline, samples with intermediate ordering will have lower corrosion current density in 3.5% NaCl.
Relative to a rapidly quenched baseline, samples with intermediate ordering will have higher compressive strength.
Oxidation, corrosion, and strength are jointly optimized only within a narrow window of processing-induced ordering.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis and boundary predict that excessive ordering can produce phase segregation and declining performance, but the falsification rule treats an ordering–segregation–performance decline correlation as falsifying the hypothesis. That result would instead support the proposed excessive-ordering branch.
